verses.1: Al-Mizan says ruʾyah can mean literal sight or knowledge. Though the verse addresses the Prophet as receiver of revelation, it addresses everyone who receives the message. Al-dīn means recompense on the Day of Judgment, making the subject one who denies the hereafter; some exegetes instead take dīn as religion.
verses.2: Al-Mizan glosses daʿʿ as harsh and violent repulsion. The fāʾ conditionally identifies those who deny retribution by its effects: they treat orphans cruelly because they fear no consequence, whereas fear would have moved them to mercy. Yaḥuḍḍu means urging people to feed the needy, a wider failure than not feeding them personally. Ṭaʿām may signal that food is almost the needy’s right (51:9), or simply mean feeding.

verses.4: Al-Mizan says sāhūn is synonymous with ghāfilūn: people who treat prayer as unimportant, miss its times, or delay it beyond its ideal time. The fāʾ makes this warning the conclusion of the preceding description, so praying people here enact denial of retribution and display hypocrisy despite feigned faith. They perform worship to be seen by people, not for God. Al-māʿūn, from ʿawn, is every useful assistance in life—such as a loan, benevolence, or lending household utensils—and the differing exegetical readings return to this general sense.
